title: Nitrate Transport, Denitrification, and Discharge in Tide‐Controlled Fractured Coastal Aquifers
content:
Abstract

Land-derived nitrate degrades coastal groundwater quality, with denitrification in intertidal aquifers serving as a critical barrier to its seaward flux. While geologic heterogeneity has been recognized as a key factor affecting nitrate transport, denitrification, and discharge in coastal aquifers, few studies have investigated how fractures regulate nitrate fate, particularly the main fractures dominating water flow. This study first integrated discrete fracture matrix model (DFM)-based sandbox experiments and numerical simulations to analyze land-sourced conservative solute transport in homogeneous, horizontally, and vertically fractured intertidal aquifers. The validated model was then scaled up to assess nitrate dynamics under point and non-point source scenarios, with sensitivity analyses further exploring how fracture geometry, aquifer hydraulic properties, and boundary conditions affect non-point source nitrate fate in horizontally fractured aquifers. Results show that main fractures act as preferential pathways directing nitrate into intertidal seawater-freshwater mixing zones, inducing denitrification hotspots at the fracture-upper saline plume (USP) interface. Under point source conditions, horizontal and vertical fractures emphasize corresponding expansion of interfacial hotspots. In the non-point source scenario, broader nitrate inputs promote denitrification near high and low tidal levels, weakening the prominence of fracture-induced hotspots. Sensitivity analyses highlight that fracture's proximity to the USP or enhanced reactant convergence capacity can expand interfacial hotspots, facilitating nitrate removal and lowering discharge concentrations. In addition, the downstream N2 plume's extent and concentration are governed by the size and activity of fracture-induced hotspots, as well as the fracture's freshwater-zone length.
